title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: The Ophthalmic Surgeon's Nightmare
summary: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage (SCH) is a devastating ocular emergency characterized by the accumulation of blood in the suprachoroidal space between the choroid and the sclera, often triggered by sudden hypotony during intraocular surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage (SCH) involves the rupture of the long or short posterior ciliary arteries, leading to rapid blood accumulation in the potential space between the choroid and the sclera. It is categorized into 'limited' (localized) or 'expulsive' (massive hemorrhage with extrusion of intraocular contents). While rare (incidence <0.2% in modern phacoemulsification), it remains one of the most vision-threatening complications in ophthalmic surgery.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: 1. Sudden Hypotony: Opening the globe or rapid drop in IOP.
2. Vascular Dilation: Choroidal vessels expand due to pressure gradient.
3. Serous Effusion: Fluid moves into suprachoroidal space.
4. Vessel Rupture: Stretch on ciliary arteries leads to shearing and rupture.
5. Massive Hemorrhage: High-pressure arterial blood fills the space.

rows: Localized, often in one or two quadrants; may resolve with medical therapy.
Involves 360 degrees; high IOP; 'kissing choroidals' on B-scan.
Ejection of vitreous, lens, or retina through surgical wound.
Occurs days after surgery, often associated with a cough or Valsalva.

sections.title: INTRAOPERATIVE RED FLAGS
content: Sudden shallowing of the anterior chamber (AC)
Rapid increase in Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
Loss of the Red Reflex (replaced by dark mass)
Hardening of the globe (stony-hard)
Prolapse of the iris, vitreous, or lens material
Severe, acute ocular pain (if patient is under local anesthesia)

branches: Slit Lamp: Shallow AC, high IOP

rows: Clear fluid, transilluminates well, low/normal IOP
Undulating membrane, no dome shape, 'tobacco dust'
Intrinsic vascularity, sentinel vessels, slow onset

sections.title: Immediate Intraoperative Management
content: Step 1: Immediate closure of all surgical incisions (Suture everything).
Step 2: Restore Intraocular Pressure using OVD (Viscoelastic) or saline.
Step 3: Administer IV Acetazolamide or Mannitol to lower IOP.
Step 4: Do NOT attempt to drain the blood immediately (arterial pressure will just refill it).
Step 5: Administer subconjunctival steroids and end the case.

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe, boring), A: AC Shallowing, I: IOP Elevation, N: No Red Reflex, S: Sudden Vision Loss.

sections.title: Postoperative Medical Therapy
content: Intensive topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h)
Systemic steroids (Prednisone 60-80mg daily) to reduce inflammation
Aggressive IOP control (Topical Beta-blockers, CAIs, Alpha-agonists)
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1%) to stabilize blood-aqueous barrier
Pain management with systemic analgesics

sections.title: Surgical Drainage Protocol
content: 1. Observation Period: Wait 7 to 14 days for clot liquefaction (Gold Standard).
2. Imaging Check: Repeat B-scan to confirm liquefaction (decreasing echogenicity).
3. Sclerotomies: Perform radial or circumferential sclerotomies in affected quadrants (usually 6-8mm from limbus).
4. AC/Vitreous Maintenance: Use an infusion cannula to maintain IOP during drainage.
5. Vitrectomy: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) often required to manage vitreous incarceration or associated RD.
6. Perfluorocarbon Liquid (PFCL): Use 'heavy water' to flatten the choroid and push blood out through sclerotomies.

sections.title: Landmark Study: AREDS and SCH
sections.content: While AREDS is for ARMD, various retrospective series (e.g., the Beaver Dam Eye Study and smaller surgical cohorts) have established that the highest risk for SCH occurs in patients with axial lengths >26mm and those undergoing combined Glaucoma-Cataract procedures. The timing of drainage was significantly influenced by the 'liquefaction study' (Hoffman et al.), advocating for the 10-14 day delay.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Phthisis Bulbi: Chronic hypotony and globe atrophy (high risk in expulsive SCH).
Tractional or Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment.
Corneal Decompensation: Due to prolonged high IOP or AC shallowing.
Chronic Secondary Glaucoma.
Prognosis: Poor if macula-involving or if expulsive; 50% achieve <20/200.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Pre-op: Always ask about Aspirin, Warfarin, or Clopidogrel. Control BP before surgery.
Intra-op: If you suspect SCH, CLOSE THE WOUND IMMEDIATELY. A single suture can save the eye.
Imaging: B-scan is the most critical tool for monitoring; serial scans show when the clot is ready for drainage.
Management: Do not rush to the OR for drainage on Day 1. Patient outcomes are better when blood has liquefied.
Differential: If the IOP is low, think Serous Effusion. If the IOP is high, think Hemorrhage.
